direct_claims: This chart shows estimated annual deaths from protein-energy malnutrition by age group for the world.
The domain is global health, nutrition, and mortality measurement.
Protein-energy malnutrition is defined here as resulting from insufficient caloric and protein intake.
The source shown is IHME, Global Burden of Disease (2025), and the chart is presented by Our World in Data.
The chart separates deaths into five age groups: under-5s, 5-14 years old, 15-49 years old, 50-69 years old, and 70+ years old.
In this field, deaths from protein-energy malnutrition represent mortality attributed to severe undernutrition from inadequate energy and protein intake.
The expert note says these estimates have wide uncertainties, especially in countries with poor vital registration, so small differences or short-term fluctuations should be interpreted cautiously.

The uncertainty warning is socially and politically important because countries with weak death registration systems may have less precise estimates, which can complicate priority setting and accountability.
The note on uncertainty means the values are estimates rather than exact counts.
derived_claims: The image indicates a time series running from about 1980 to 2023. — derived by reading the x-axis labels in the chart image.
The largest share of deaths appears to come from under-5s for most or all of the period shown. — derived by comparing stacked age-band contributions across the chart image.

The chart suggests a long-term global decline in total deaths from protein-energy malnutrition from the early 1980s to 2023, despite some sharp temporary increases. — derived by reading the overall stacked total trend across time in the chart image.
One pronounced peak occurs in the early 1980s, and another smaller spike appears around 2011. — derived by identifying local maxima from the chart image.

The under-5 category declines substantially over time, while the 70+ category becomes a more noticeable share of the remaining total in later years. — derived by comparing age-group contributions at the beginning versus end of the series in the chart image.

The chart indicates that children under five bear the largest burden, so policies affecting maternal nutrition, infant feeding, food access, vaccination, and primary care are likely to be especially relevant. — derived in part from under-5s being the largest age-group contribution in the chart image; policy implications rely on public health knowledge.

The global decline over time suggests that progress against extreme malnutrition is possible, but the remaining deaths indicate that it has not been eliminated. — derived by reading the long-term decline and nonzero endpoint from the chart image.

If future shocks such as conflict, economic crisis, food-price spikes, or health-system disruption occur, malnutrition deaths could rise again, as temporary spikes in the series show that reversals are possible. — derived in part from temporary spikes visible in the chart image; proposed drivers rely on humanitarian and public health knowledge.
